newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: CRICKET-ONLY RAIN OR ANOTHER HOUDINI ACT CAN SAVE NZ.
newsitem.headline: CRICKET-ONLY RAIN OR ANOTHER HOUDINI ACT CAN SAVE NZ.

text.p: Only rain or another desperate bottom order batting escape can save New Zealand against England after another batting collapse before lunch on the last day of the second test on Monday.
Requiring 259 to make England bat a second time, New Zealand were 177 for eight at the interval, with Chris Cairns, the only remaining batsman of note, on 12 and Geoff Allott yet to score.
Fast-medium Darren Gough proved the destroyer for England. In a withering five-over burst he took four wickets for 11 runs to chop through New Zealand's middle order.
With five for 40 in the first test Gough is in line to pick up a 10 wicket bag.
He had captain Lee Germon play onto his stumps to his fourth ball of the day, then had stubborn Blair Pocock brilliantly caught at second slip by Nick Knight for 64 in his next over.

First test century-maker Nathan Astle's uncomfortable stay was ended by a superb diving catch by wicketkeeper Alec Stewart and three balls later Simon Doull's awful push at a ball outside his off stump gave Knight his second catch of the innings.
Play was half an hour late starting, due to light early morning rain, but after Pocock and Germon's diligent fifth-wicket stand of 36 had been broken, there was little further resistance.
Pocock batted for 339 minutes, faced 270 balls and hit five fours in a defiant performance.
Gough received excellent support from seamer Andrew Caddick, who bowled beautifully but without luck.
New Zealand escaped with a draw in the first test after Astle and world record test duck holder Danny Morrison batted over three hours in a record tenth wicket stand for New Zealand against England.
The weather was gloomy in Wellington and rain may be a better bet than New Zealand's batsmen to save the test.
A win here would deflect criticism from England captain Mike Atherton after he was attacked for drawing the test series in the first leg of the tour in Zimbabwe and losing the one day series there.
Instead, the heat may go on Germon and the New Zealanders who have been criticised for partying into the early hours of the morning during this test and for their spineless batting displays.
